title: Success criteria: start, during and handover
blurb: Explain what success criteria are and why they matter at the start, during delivery and at handover.
question: At the closure meeting for a school IT refresh, the finance director says the project succeeded because it came in under budget. The head teacher says it failed because teachers still can't use the new kit. What should have been agreed at the start, and how would it have helped all the way through?

teach.h: How will we know we've succeeded?
teach.body: Success criteria are the qualitative or quantitative measures by which the success of the project is judged. In plain English: the agreed answer to 'what does good look like?', written down before work starts. Quantitative criteria are numbers (within budget, live by a date, 95% uptime). Qualitative criteria are judgements (users find it easier to use). Good projects use both.

teach.h: Three moments when success criteria matter

steps.label: At the start
steps.sub: Agree what success looks like; guide planning and trade-offs; align stakeholders

steps.label: During delivery
steps.sub: Monitor performance against them; steer decisions

steps.label: At handover
steps.sub: Judge success; support acceptance and closure; capture lessons

teach.caption: Set once, used throughout: they are the thread that links planning, control and closure.

teach.h: What they do at each stage
Why agree them at the start
teach.body: If success isn't agreed up front, each stakeholder quietly judges the project by their own measure, and you only find out at the end. Agreeing criteria at the start gives one shared definition of success, guides planning, and tells the team which of time, cost, quality and scope matters most when trade-offs come. 'On time and on budget' alone is rarely enough.

Before work started, the sponsor agreed four success criteria with the head teacher, finance director and staff. During the summer installation, the PM tracked progress against them each week. When a supplier delay forced a choice between cutting teacher training or slipping go-live by a week, the criteria (teacher confidence ranked high) guided the decision. At handover, results were assessed against the same four measures.

head: Criterion
Type
How it is judged
teach.caption: A mix of numbers and judgements, agreed with everyone who will decide whether the project worked.

teach.h: During delivery: steer by the criteria
teach.caption: If the criteria themselves stop being relevant, revise them formally with the stakeholders rather than quietly dropping them.

teach.h: Three measures that are easily confused

teach.text: Exam traps: success criteria are NOT set at closure (they are agreed at the start), they are NOT acceptance criteria (those apply to individual outputs) and they are NOT just 'on time and on budget'. They also don't remove the need for governance, a business case or reporting.

items: Success criteria: the qualitative or quantitative measures by which project success is judged.
Start: agree what success looks like, guide planning, priorities and trade-offs, align stakeholders.
During: monitor performance against them and steer decisions.
Handover: assess whether the project succeeded, support acceptance and closure, capture lessons.

summary: You can now define success criteria and explain their job at each stage: agreeing and aligning at the start, monitoring and steering during delivery, and judging success, supporting acceptance and capturing lessons at handover. You can also tell them apart from acceptance criteria and KPIs.

A.q: Which of the following best describes success criteria?
options: Standards that a single output must meet to be accepted
Indicators used to track ongoing operational performance
Measures by which the success of the project is judged
Conditions that must be true before the work can start
A.why: Success criteria are the qualitative or quantitative measures by which the project's success is judged.

whyNot.0: Standards for a single output are acceptance criteria.
whyNot.1: Indicators tracking ongoing performance are KPIs.
whyNot.3: Conditions that must hold before work starts are prerequisites or assumptions.

A.q: What is the main reason for agreeing success criteria at the start of a project?
options: So stakeholders share one definition of success
So the business case no longer needs to be written
So the budget can never be changed during delivery
So the sponsor can step away from the project early
A.why: Agreeing criteria at the start aligns stakeholders on what success looks like and guides planning and trade-offs.

whyNot.1: The business case is still needed to justify the investment.
whyNot.2: Budgets can still change through change control.

A.q: At handover, how are the agreed success criteria mainly used?
options: To decide which team members are released first
To confirm the business case is no longer required
To replace the final report with a short checklist
To assess whether the project achieved what was agreed
A.why: At handover, results are assessed against the agreed criteria to judge success and support acceptance and closure.

whyNot.0: Releasing staff is a resourcing decision, not the purpose of success criteria.
whyNot.1: The business case continues to matter for benefits realisation.
whyNot.2: Closure still needs reporting; criteria inform it rather than replace it.

B.q: During deployment, what is the main role of the success criteria?
options: Setting the organisation's strategic objectives
Monitoring performance and steering decisions
Replacing the progress reports to the sponsor
Defining the work packages in the breakdown
B.why: During delivery, performance is monitored against the success criteria and they steer decisions such as trade-offs.

whyNot.0: Strategy is set by the organisation, above the project.
whyNot.2: Progress reporting is still needed; criteria give it a reference point.
whyNot.3: Work packages come from the work breakdown structure.

B.q: Which of the following is a QUALITATIVE success criterion?
options: Delivered within the £200k budget
Live by the end of March
Users find the portal easier to use
Page response under two seconds
B.why: A judgement of how users feel about the portal is qualitative; the others are measurable numbers.

whyNot.1: A date is a quantitative, time-based measure.
whyNot.3: A response time is a quantitative technical measure.

B.q: Which statement correctly contrasts success criteria with acceptance criteria?
options: Success criteria judge the project; acceptance criteria judge outputs
Acceptance criteria judge the project; success criteria judge outputs
Both are set at closure to decide whether the sponsor signs off
Both are key performance indicators tracked by the PMO monthly
B.why: Success criteria judge the success of the project as a whole; acceptance criteria are the conditions an individual output must meet.

whyNot.2: Both should be agreed early, not at closure.
whyNot.3: KPIs track ongoing performance; neither is simply a KPI.

C.q: At closure, one director says the project succeeded because it was on budget; another says it failed because sales did not rise. What would most likely have prevented this?
options: A longer and more detailed risk register
Holding the post-project review sooner
Releasing the project team more slowly
Agreeing success criteria at the outset
C.why: Agreed success criteria at the start give one shared definition of success, avoiding conflicting judgements at the end.

whyNot.0: A risk register manages uncertainty; it doesn't define success.
whyNot.1: A review captures lessons; it can't fix an undefined target after the event.
whyNot.2: Team release timing has no bearing on what counts as success.

C.q: A supplier delay forces a choice: cut user training or slip go-live by a week. The agreed success criteria rank user confidence above the go-live date. How do the criteria help?
options: They allow the PM to skip discussing it with anyone
They show which choice better serves agreed success
They automatically approve whichever option is cheaper
They replace the change control process for the choice
C.why: During delivery, success criteria steer decisions and trade-offs towards what stakeholders agreed matters most.

whyNot.0: Significant trade-offs still need the right people involved, such as the sponsor.
whyNot.2: Criteria guide judgement; they don't automatically pick the cheapest option.
whyNot.3: Changes to the baseline still go through change control.

C.q: Which THREE of the following are reasons to use success criteria at handover? 1. Assess whether the project succeeded 2. Support acceptance and closure 3. Capture lessons for future projects 4. Set the project budget
options: 1, 2 and 3
1, 2 and 4
1, 3 and 4
2, 3 and 4
C.why: At handover, success criteria are used to assess success, support acceptance and closure, and capture lessons.

whyNot.1: The budget is set in planning, not at handover.
whyNot.2: Setting the budget is not a handover use of success criteria.
whyNot.3: The budget was set long before handover.

reteach.title: Think of planning a wedding
reteach.question: A couple plan their wedding with two sets of parents involved. What happens if nobody agrees up front what a 'successful' day means?

blocks.h: Agree 'a great day' before booking anything
blocks.body: One parent thinks success is staying within £15k. Another wants all 120 relatives invited. The couple just want a relaxed day. If they agree these up front, every choice (venue, guest list, caterer) can be checked against them. On the day, they can tell whether it went to plan. Afterwards, they can honestly judge it, and pass tips on to a sibling.

blocks.h: The wedding's success criteria over time

blocks.text: Agreeing what 'success' means on the morning after is too late: everyone already has a different answer. The same is true at project closure.

explain.body: The qualitative or quantitative measures by which the success of the project is judged. Use a mix: numbers such as cost and dates, and judgements such as user satisfaction.

test.q: Success criteria can be expressed in which form?
options: Quantitative measures only
Qualitative measures only
Qualitative or quantitative
Financial measures only
test.why: Success criteria may be qualitative or quantitative, and a good set usually includes both.

whyNot.0: Numbers alone miss things like satisfaction.
whyNot.1: Judgements alone can be hard to assess objectively.
whyNot.3: Cost is only one kind of measure; time, quality and satisfaction matter too.

explain.body: Agree what success looks like with key stakeholders. This aligns expectations, guides planning, and sets priorities for later trade-offs between time, cost, quality and scope.

test.q: How does agreeing success criteria at the start help with later trade-offs?
options: It means trade-offs are never needed
It fixes the scope so it cannot change
It shows which priorities matter most
It lets the team make all the decisions
test.why: Agreed criteria reveal stakeholders' priorities, which guide trade-offs when time, cost, quality and scope compete.

whyNot.0: Trade-offs still arise; criteria help resolve them.
whyNot.1: Scope can still change through change control.
whyNot.3: Significant decisions still involve the sponsor and stakeholders.

explain.body: Monitor performance against the criteria and use them to steer decisions. If they stop being relevant, revise and agree them formally with stakeholders rather than abandoning them.

test.q: Partway through delivery, an original success criterion is no longer relevant. What is the best course of action?
options: Drop it quietly and carry on
Keep using it whatever happens
Let the team choose a new one
Revise and agree it formally
test.why: Criteria should stay relevant, so they are revised and formally agreed with key stakeholders.

whyNot.0: Dropping it without agreement breaks the shared definition of success.
whyNot.1: An irrelevant criterion would steer the project in the wrong direction.
whyNot.2: The criteria belong to the stakeholders, not the team alone.

explain.body: Assess whether the project succeeded against the agreed criteria, use them to support acceptance and closure, and capture lessons on what helped or hindered success.

test.q: At closure, a team wants to confirm the project achieved what it set out to do. What should it refer to?
options: The work breakdown structure for the build
The success criteria agreed at the start
The configuration records for each item
The resource histogram for the deployment
test.why: The success criteria agreed at the start are the benchmark for judging whether the project succeeded.

whyNot.0: The WBS defines the work, not whether the project succeeded.
whyNot.2: Configuration records track item versions and status.
whyNot.3: A resource histogram shows resource usage over time.
